messages.subject: struggling with categorical lmer (again)
messages.body_plain:
Hi R-peers,

 

I was just analyzing a data set that looked at the effect of visual speech
under a blocked and a mixed condition.

(Don't bother what this means). The results were quite clear, the effect of
the visual signal was much less in the mixed conditions.

If I put the results as percentage of /b/ responses, the result was

 

Blocked Condition:          visual /b/: 68% visual /d/: 21% 

Mixed Condition:             visual /b/: 54%  visual /d/: 55%

 

You would expect this huge effect to give rise to a clear interaction, and
while the beta weight for visualCue x condition was quite large,

the significance level was only 0.04 in a glmer (See the formula for the
lmer below), which is somewhat surprising given the huge effect in the
descriptive data.

(In fact, if we always found such clear effects, we probably would not need
statistics at all.)

 

So, I thought, maybe there are huge inter-individual differences, but no, if
I look at the means for the 10 participants,
and calculate the difference in percentage /b/ responses for the two visual
conditions (visual /b/ and visual /d/) I get the following:

(Yes, I should use logOdds for that, but I stay with percentages here, for
ease of presentation)

 


blocked

mixed


45

0


35

3


51

3


49

-9


76

-1


39

-1


70

-1


20

1


48

-1


39

-6

 

 

This looks like a pretty consistent effect over subjects, and does not rhyme
well with the barely significant effect from the glmer.

 

There is one reason I can see for that: The design was not balanced in terms
of visual and auditory cues. Because we thought that

the incongruent trials (visual cue different from auditory cue) would
produce more noise, we actually used more of those than congruent trials.

(So, that in fact, the cell means would be estimated with roughly similar
precision.)

 

Therefore, the visual and auditory cues are not independent in the overall
analysis, since visual = /b/ makes it more likely that audio = /d/.

(Since there are more incongruent trials.)  But I would have thought that
having a regression weight for "auditoryCue" would take care of that.

Is the reason the glmer does not really reflect this huge and consistent
effect? Any other ideas why the glmer may find this barely significant?

 

Kind regards,

Holger

 

P.S.: This is how the glmer was specified:

 

all.lmer = glmer(response ~ audCueC + visCueC*partC + (1|subject) +
(0+visCueC|subject) + (0+audCueC|subject)+(0 + partC|subject) + (0 +
partC:visCueC|subject)  , data = all2, family = "binomial")

 

Notes

-          I used uncorrelated random slopes, since this is more likely to
converge. 

-          All predictors are binary coded as -0.5 versus 0.5, so that the
regression weight gives an effect size.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Holger,

Two quick knee-jerk thoughts:

1. 10 people is a pretty small sample!  A power analysis might tell you
just how huge the effect would need to be to be significant at p < .05.

2. Uncorrelated effects can help the model converge (usually), because in
essence it means the model need to estimate fewer parameters, but it also
means that your model forces all of the random effects to be uncorrelated.
That is, the degree to which some subjects might be overall more accurate
(random effect on the intercept) is forced to be completely uncorrelated
with the degree to which some subjects display a bigger effect of visCueC,
and so on.  Depending on how well this assumption actually fits the data
could be leading to a converging-but-misfitting model, which could have
some weird impacts on the effect estimation.

So, I think this all boils down to a pretty common problem: you may just
not have enough data, especially to support estimation of a pretty complex
model.

hope that helps,
-scott

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

 

Thanks for your responses. Here are my thoughts:

 

1.       Small Sample size

While I agree that 10 people is a small sample for your average pyschLing study, I think it is wrong to assume that each study needs the same number of participants.

This  is a more psychophysical experiment, where an n = 10 is quite appropriate, due to the fact that there is no item variance

(only one item) and that there are quite a large number of observations per participant per cell (20-40 in my case).

If my memory is not deceiving me, this is also the typical n you would find in the examples of the “Signal detection theory: A user’s guide” book.

 

2.       The point is not so much to get things significant or not. 

I was mainly surprised because of the low level of significance  that glmer gave me. 

If I run the same data through an ANOVA using logOdds of the proportions, I actually get an F value of (F1,9) = 136 for the same interaction

which is somewhere in the significant range. And the model is not super complex, it is a 3-factor experiment, with 8 condition means (each factor being binary). 

So, maybe, to restate the question:

 

How can it be that an ANOVA on a pretty straightforward experimental data set tells me: “Yes, that effect is definitely there”

while the glmer says something like “there might be something, but it may go away if you test another 4 participants”.

 

3.       To give  more information, the complete model output is pasted below

A model with correlated parameters actually does converge with pretty similar results. Again, I do not really care about the specifics of this data set,
it is more the problem of the huge discrepancy what the data look like, with loads of consistency over subjects but glmer indicating an unclear effect.

 

4.       Correlated versus uncorrelated random effects

I am starting to get confused about this. I always thought that using the (0 + ... | subject) syntax only meant that the correlation was not estimated as a model parameter,

not that the correlation is forced to be zero. But this is what Scott indicated, and it might be correct.

However, I just checked that by using  “cor(ranef(all.lmer)$subject)”, (giving me the correlation matrix for the subject random effects.

With this, I find huge correlations between some random slopes.

This seems to suggest that the (0 + ..... |subject) syntax does not force the random slopes to be uncorrelated. 

Is this correct, or is my simple test here wrong?

messages.body_plain:
The random effects are uncorrelated in the model, which is not to say that
the BLUPs are uncorrelated when the model is applied to this data.
(Similarly, the random effects are always normally distributed in the
model, which is not to say that any set of BLUPs is normally distributed.)

Agree with original post that something is 'wrong' here, subjects barely
vary with respect to this interaction, so why isn't the p-value much lower?
Can you get it to converge (to see what happens, as part of the
investigation) by ignoring the auditory cue (either splitting the data, or
just ignoring it) and using the ordinary syntax, that is to say, visCueC *
partC + (visCueC * partC|subject)?

messages.subject: Re: struggling with categorical lmer (again)
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the nice discussion!

1. I didn't mean "atypically small"; as you point out, this is pretty
typical.  I just meant it might be too small for the model you're trying to
fit.

2. It's hard to answer "why is ANOVA giving clearly sig results, while
glmer isn't", because there are a lot of differences between those models,
and how they're getting estimated. lt could be a lot of things.  And your
analysis/data probably violates some of the assumptions from either of
those kinds of models.  But which one is violated worse, or which model is
more appropriate, well, that gets pretty tricky.  Maybe some simulation
studies could help suss that out, but I think that may be too much of an
investment for this data.

3. Good to know!  Then my second guess is probably not super relevant here.

4. Hmm, this is interesting.  AFAIK, "not estimating" the correlations is
the same as "constraining" the correlations, and when you constrain these
in lmer, you are constraining them to be uncorrelated, i.e., r = 0.  The
fact that your empirical check on the ranefs look pretty different from
zero may be telling, or not.  With lmer, there is a difference between the
estimated parameters and the ranefs.  For example, the variance of each
random effect is an estimated parameter (and adds to the df of the overall
model), but if you use ranef(), you are actually getting the BLUPs, which
are not estimated parameters.  And if you check the variance of the BLUPs,
it's not exactly equal to the estimated variance of the random effect.
This is not (AFAIK) a paradox of any kind, just related to how the BLUPs
are calculated.  So when you do the cor(ranef) trick, you are looking at
the correlations between the BLUPs, which is NOT the same as the
correlation parameters.  Unless I have gravely misunderstood something
(always a possibility), the fact that they are not estimated means that the
the correlation parameters are constrained to be zero.  What's interesting
is that the BLUP correlations can end up wildly different from zero.
Whether that "means" something  or not, I'm not sure.

But given the estimated std dev of the interaction (close to 1, larger than
the interaction effect itself), it doesn't seem very weird that it would be
"barely" significant.  Even if it's "typical", it's a pretty small N for 5
fixed parameters and 5 random effect parameters, when those ranefs are
being estimated from just 10 people.

-scott

messages.subject: Best models for stress data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi list members,
I'm revising a paper where some colleagues and I worked with archival
recordings to try to determine evidence for the position of lexical stress
(and in
particular, whether stress is on the initial syllable, or on
phonemically long vowels). We did this in the original paper with
paired t-tests (comparing F0, intensity, duration, and
centralization), with a correction for multiple testing. There is
ample precedent for this in the phonetics literature, although we are
well aware that this makes simplifying assumptions (e.g. about the
independence of the variables we are looking at).
A reviewer has insisted that we instead use a mixed effects model,
though they don't seem to give any reasons for this other than "this
is what people do nowadays". The stress analyses that I have seen
using lme4, for example, take stress as a fixed effect. We can't do
that, because we don't have independent judgements of where stress is.
That is, rather than asking "what are the significant acoustic
correlates of stress in this language", we are asking "for each of
these well-known correlates of stress, which syllable positions
pattern together?"
I'd be interested in your opinions about the best way to proceed here,
whether we should simply cite precedents for our methods, or compare
competing models of stress placement, or something else.
Claire

-- 

Claire Bowern
Associate Professor
Director of Graduate Studies
Department of Linguistics
370 Temple St, Rm 313
New Haven, CT  06511

Hello Daniel,

 

So I tried what you suggested (a model without the auditory parameter):

response ~ visCueC * partC + (1 + visCueC *  partC | subject)

 

The model converges without the auditory predictor

and then the interaction is there where you would expect it:

 

visCueC:partC -2.37547    0.40580  -5.854 4.81e-09 ***

 

Actually, using uncorrelated random effects makes a huge difference

visCueC:partC -2.30952    0.31356  -7.365 1.77e-13 ***,

with four orders of magnitude on the p-value,

but only in a part of the coordinate system, where we do not really care about it.

 

Given this result, I further investigated the role of the unbalance design.

To remind everyone, in each condition, each participant had the following trials numbers 

                aud /b/                 aud /d/

visual

/b/         20                           40

/d/         40                           20

 

(This was not by accident, but based on the idea that the cell means of these incongruent trials would be more difficult to measure.)

 

I tested the role of that by randomly rejecting half of the incongruent trials of each subject and condition.

And then I get a result that kind of meets the expectation:

 

Fixed effects:

              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    

(Intercept)          -0.05298    0.10012  -0.529  0.59667    

audCueC              -0.37555    0.13241  -2.836  0.00456 ** 

visCueC                1.06206    0.16581   6.405 1.50e-10 ***

partC                     0.57009    0.38818   1.469  0.14193    

visCueC:partC    -2.41119    0.41463  -5.815 6.05e-09 ***

 

This probably means I have to have another good look at Wurm’s paper on the counter-intuitive effects of residualizing,

because this is what happens in the earlier model: First, there is the effect of auditory model is accounted for, and then 
the other effects deal with the rest. 

 

Kind regards,

Holger

The random effects are uncorrelated in the model, which is not to say that the BLUPs are uncorrelated when the model is applied to this data. (Similarly, the random effects are always normally distributed in the model, which is not to say that any set of BLUPs is normally distributed.)

 

Agree with original post that something is 'wrong' here, subjects barely vary with respect to this interaction, so why isn't the p-value much lower? Can you get it to converge (to see what happens, as part of the investigation) by ignoring the auditory cue (either splitting the data, or just ignoring it) and using the ordinary syntax, that is to say, visCueC * partC + (visCueC * partC|subject)?

 

On Fri, Feb 13, 2015 at 10:55 AM, Holger Mitterer <holger.mitterer-Mj5aoWcxWbpeoWH0uzbU5w at public.gmane.org <mailto:holger.mitterer-Mj5aoWcxWbpeoWH0uzbU5w at public.gmane.org> > wrote:

Hi R-peers,

 

I was just analyzing a data set that looked at the effect of visual speech under a blocked and a mixed condition.

(Don’t bother what this means). The results were quite clear, the effect of the visual signal was much less in the mixed conditions.

If I put the results as percentage of /b/ responses, the result was

 

Blocked Condition:          visual /b/: 68% visual /d/: 21% 

Mixed Condition:             visual /b/: 54%  visual /d/: 55%

 

You would expect this huge effect to give rise to a clear interaction, and while the beta weight for visualCue x condition was quite large,

the significance level was only 0.04 in a glmer (See the formula for the lmer below), which is somewhat surprising given the huge effect in the descriptive data.

(In fact, if we always found such clear effects, we probably would not need statistics at all.)

 

So, I thought, maybe there are huge inter-individual differences, but no, if I look at the means for the 10 participants,
and calculate the difference in percentage /b/ responses for the two visual conditions (visual /b/ and visual /d/) I get the following:

(Yes, I should use logOdds for that, but I stay with percentages here, for ease of presentation)

 


blocked

mixed


45

0


35

3


51

3


49

-9


76

-1


39

-1


70

-1


20

1


48

-1


39

-6

 

 

This looks like a pretty consistent effect over subjects, and does not rhyme well with the barely significant effect from the glmer.

 

There is one reason I can see for that: The design was not balanced in terms of visual and auditory cues. Because we thought that

the incongruent trials (visual cue different from auditory cue) would produce more noise, we actually used more of those than congruent trials.

(So, that in fact, the cell means would be estimated with roughly similar precision.)

 

Therefore, the visual and auditory cues are not independent in the overall analysis, since visual = /b/ makes it more likely that audio = /d/.

(Since there are more incongruent trials.)  But I would have thought that having a regression weight for “auditoryCue” would take care of that.

Is the reason the glmer does not really reflect this huge and consistent effect? Any other ideas why the glmer may find this barely significant?

 

Kind regards,

Holger

 

P.S.: This is how the glmer was specified:

 

all.lmer = glmer(response ~ audCueC + visCueC*partC + (1|subject) + (0+visCueC|subject) + (0+audCueC|subject)+(0 + partC|subject) + (0 + partC:visCueC|subject)  , data = all2, family = "binomial")

 

Notes

-          I used uncorrelated random slopes, since this is more likely to converge. 

-          All predictors are binary coded as -0.5 versus 0.5, so that the regression weight gives an effect size.

messages.subject: Best models for stress data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Claire,
I infer that the archival recordings didn't come with native speaker
judgments about stress placement, or else you wouldn't be asking this
question. But thinking about how you would model it if you *did* have a
priori information about stress (and were investigating which acoustic
measures were correlates) can point the way to how you might answer the
question without such a priori information.  If you knew stress position,
you could use the native speaker judgment as the (binary) outcome you're
trying to predict, and using the four acoustic measures as the predictors.
This would be something like:

speakerSaysItsStressed ~ fzero + intens + dur + centr

This would be an ordinary GLM, not a mixed model, though you could include
a random effect for "word" or "speaker" if you have several replicates of
each word, or several different speakers (or both). Given this model
specification, you could create variables to represent your two hypotheses,
and run one model for each, then compare model fit.  In other words, a
vector called "initialStress" with 1s for all data points that are initial
syllables (and 0s elsewhere), and a vector called "lengthEqualsStress" with
1s for all the syllables with long vowels (and 0s elsewhere).  Then the two
models are

initialStress ~ fzero + intens + dur + centr
lengthEqualsStress ~ fzero + intens + dur + centr

Hope that helps,
-- dan

Daniel McCloy
http://dan.mccloy.info/
Postdoctoral Research Fellow
Institute for Learning and Brain Sciences
University of Washington

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

 

I have a question concerning correlated random effects. Following Barr et al., I fitted my model with a maximal random effect structure:

 

e1=glmer(Response~cGroup*cAccent+(1|Subject)+(cGroup*cAccent+1|Item),E1,family="binomial")

 

However, the model failed to converge. So I next removed the correlation between item slopes and item intercept.

 

e1b=glmer(Response~cGroup*cAccent+(1|Subject)+(cGroup*cAccent+0|Item)+(1|Item),E1,family="binomial")

 

I hope the above is the right way of doing it in the new glmer. The model output suggests that there were strong correlations among the random slopes; and also, the variance for cAccent and the interaction item slope seemed to be very small.

 

Random effects:

Groups  Name           Variance Std.Dev. Corr       

 Subject (Intercept)    0.12143  0.3485              

 Item    cGroup         1.20142  1.0961              

         cAccent        0.08034  0.2834   -0.97      

         cGroup:cAccent 0.05026  0.2242    0.97 -1.00

Item.1  (Intercept)    1.92902  1.3889              

Number of obs: 2110, groups:  Subject, 120; Item, 22

 

Fixed effects:

               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    

(Intercept)     0.08724    0.30595   0.285   0.7755    

cGroup          2.88675    0.28489  10.133   <2e-16 ***

cAccent         0.29064    0.14806   1.963   0.0496 *  

cGroup:cAccent -0.48178    0.27544  -1.749   0.0803 .  

---

Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

 

 

I wonder whether it matters to have highly correlated random effects. I seem to have read that these may cause problems. If they do, how to remedy this? Also, is it OK to get rid of random slopes with near-zero variances (sounds anti-Barr though).

 

Thanks for any help,

 

Zhenguang Cai
